To understand "indefinite," first understand its opposite: definite.

Something definite is clear, exact, certain, and fixed. You know exactly what it is, when it ends, or what it means. No confusion, no vagueness.

Now add "in-" to the front, which simply means "not."

So indefinite means: not clear, not exact, not certain, and not fixed. Whenever something is blurry, open-ended, vague, or without a known boundary — it is indefinite.

That single idea — the absence of clear definition or limit — is the heart of this word. Everything else is just that same idea applied to different situations.

1. Vague or Unclear (in description)

When something is indefinite, you cannot pin it down precisely. It has no sharp edges — it's fuzzy, ambiguous, or hard to describe exactly.

  • "She gave an indefinite answer."
    She didn't say yes or no clearly. Her answer was somewhere in between, leaving you unsure.
  • "The shape of the cloud was indefinite."
    You couldn't say exactly what shape it was — it kept shifting, and it had no clean outline.
  • "He had an indefinite sense of unease."
    He felt uneasy, but he couldn't quite say why or describe it precisely.

In this use, indefinite ≈ vague, unclear, imprecise. The thing exists, but its exact nature is blurry or hard to define.

2. Without a Fixed Limit or End (in time or amount)

This is the most common everyday use of the word. When something — especially a period of time, a plan, or a number — has no set endpoint or boundary, it is indefinite.

  • "The project has been postponed for an indefinite period."
    Nobody knows when the project will restart. There is no date. It could be weeks, months, or years — no one can say.
  • "She was placed on indefinite leave."
    She was sent on leave with no fixed return date.
  • "The borders were closed indefinitely."
    The borders were closed, and no date was given for when they would reopen. The closure had no known end.
  • "He waited for an indefinite amount of time."
    We don't know how long he waited — it was not specified.

In this use, indefinite ≈ open-ended, with no set limit, for an unknown duration. It does not mean "forever" — it simply means the end point hasn't been decided or is unknown yet.

Important nuance: Indefinite does not always mean "bad" or "permanent." It just means the limit hasn't been set. A situation called indefinite can still end — we just don't know when.

In English grammar, "indefinite" describes words that point to something general or non-specific, rather than one particular thing.

Indefinite Articles: a and an

The words a and an are called indefinite articles because they do not point to a specific thing.

  • "I want a book." → Any book. Not a particular one.
  • "She adopted a dog." → Some dog. We don't know which one yet.

Compare this to the (the definite article), which points to something specific:

  • "I want the book." → That specific book we both know about.

So: a/an = indefinite (not specific) | the = definite (specific).

Indefinite Pronouns

These are words like someone, anyone, nobody, everything, something, anywhere, whoever, whatever, etc. They are called "indefinite" because they refer to people or things without specifying exactly who or what.

  • "Someone called for you." → We don't know who. No specific person is named.
  • "Anything will do." → No specific thing is required — whatever is available is fine.
  • "Nobody came." → No specific person is mentioned — just a general statement about everyone.

These words are indefinite because they are deliberately non-specific or general.
The One Thread Running Through All Uses

No matter the context, "indefinite" always signals the same thing: something is not clearly or precisely defined — whether it's an idea that's vague, a time limit that hasn't been set, or a word that refers to nothing specific.

If you stood in front of a photograph that was slightly out of focus — not completely blurry, but not sharp either — that blurriness is the feeling of "indefinite." Something is there. You can sense it. But its edges, its exact form, its precise limits — those aren't clear.

Whenever something lacks that sharpness and precision — in time, in meaning, in language, in form — the right word for it is indefinite.
